Starlink.purpose: SpaceX’s own low-orbit internet network. These satellites relay broadband to user terminals; some variants also connect ordinary mobile phones through partner networks.
Starlink.example: A batch builds network capacity, but release is followed by checkout and orbital positioning.

Communications.purpose: Communications is a job, not one technology: satellite radio, mobile voice/data and internet broadband all sit in this group. These are customer spacecraft, separate from the Starlink category.
Communications.example: SiriusXM broadcasts audio; Thuraya provides mobile satellite connectivity; Amazon’s Kuiper builds a competing broadband constellation.

Security & navigation.purpose: Government missions include navigation and timing, military communications and reconnaissance. GPS serves civilian as well as military users; it is not an internet constellation.
Security & navigation.example: GPS III SV08 is a navigation spacecraft. Classified missions can have less public detail, so unknown payload specifics stay unknown.

Rideshare.purpose: Many customers share one rocket instead of each buying a dedicated launch. Their spacecraft can do different jobs: imaging, experiments, communications or technology demonstrations.
Rideshare.example: Transporter and Bandwagon are booking formats, not satellite types. A high object count need not mean a heavy payload.

Science & weather.purpose: Observatories collect measurements of Earth, the Sun or the wider universe. They deliver scientific data rather than a consumer connectivity service.
Science & weather.example: SPHEREx studies the infrared sky; PUNCH’s four spacecraft observe how the Sun’s outer atmosphere becomes solar wind.

Moon missions.purpose: Robotic spacecraft travel beyond Earth orbit to deliver experiments or explore the lunar environment. Launch success and landing success are separate events.
Moon missions.example: Blue Ghost carried 10 NASA science and technology instruments under the commercial lunar delivery program.

Crew.purpose: Dragon carries people, life-support systems and return capability. Some flights visit the station; others are independent missions. Capsule mass is not the mass of its passengers.
Crew.example: Fram2 targeted a polar orbit rather than a station docking mission.

Station cargo.purpose: Resupply vehicles carry experiments, food, equipment and other logistics to the space station. Spacecraft mass and useful cargo mass are different quantities.
Station cargo.example: Dragon CRS missions and the Cygnus resupply flight are grouped here; small hosted payloads can share the trip.

Starship tests.purpose: Development flights test the launch system, propulsion, flight control and recovery. They are not equivalent to an operational satellite-delivery service.
Starship tests.example: The 2025 tests carried Starlink simulators. Those test objects do not count as real Starlink satellites in this overview.

2025-001.title: A phone-and-data network, not home broadband
2025-001.text: Thuraya-4 NGS supports mobile satellite communications. It is a different service architecture from a low-orbit Starlink batch, even though both can carry data.

2025-122.title: The payload behind satellite radio
2025-122.text: SiriusXM’s SXM-10 broadcasts digital audio. Its operator announced operational service in August 2025, after launch and in-orbit testing—a concrete example of why “launched” does not mean “already serving.”

2025-151.title: SpaceX launched a broadband rival
2025-151.text: Amazon’s first Falcon 9 Kuiper mission carried 24 satellites. The customer’s internet constellation competes with Starlink, while SpaceX also supplies its launch service.

2025-171.title: Another customer constellation
2025-171.text: This flight carried another 24 Amazon Kuiper satellites in the GCAT ledger. Customer broadband payloads are kept separate from SpaceX’s internal Starlink missions.

2025-228.title: Same launcher, different network
2025-228.text: The catalog records 24 Amazon Kuiper satellites on this flight. Communications payloads are not automatically Starlinks just because they ride a Falcon 9.

2025-047.title: One launch, two views of the cosmos
2025-047.text: SPHEREx maps the infrared sky. PUNCH uses four smaller spacecraft to study the transition from the solar corona to the solar wind. Five catalogued spacecraft share one science flight.

2025-010.title: A Moon-bound flight, not a satellite shell
2025-010.text: Blue Ghost shared this launch with the Resilience lander. Blue Ghost’s 10 NASA instruments were part of a commercial lunar delivery; liftoff was the beginning of the mission, not its final milestone.

2025-066.title: A different destination for a crew
2025-066.text: Fram2’s four-person Dragon mission targeted a 90-degree polar orbit, rather than a visit to the International Space Station. Crew missions can have very different routes and objectives.

2025-116.title: The clock behind a location fix
2025-116.text: GPS III SV08 belongs to the navigation and timing system. GPS signals support civilian navigation and precise timing as well as military use; this is not a broadband delivery satellite.

launchContracts.scope: Launch service and other mission-related costs. Published award; not SpaceX internal cost or necessarily final spend.
Firm-fixed-price award including launch services and other mission-related costs. Not a bare rocket price.
